primary_text_note: Novel in copyright. Verified against litcharts.com/lit/anita-and-me (summary, quotes, characters, chapter-1, chapter-13), gradesaver.com/anita-and-me (summary, character-list) and the OCR J352 spec. WebSearch budget exhausted; several LitCharts chapter pages returned empty bodies.

findings.claim: “OCR’s Component 01 Section A tests your ability… For both parts, AO3 (context) is assessed” (also in knowledge_checks[3].q and the key-fact revision tip).
findings.truth: Two faults. (a) “Component 01” is a banned spec code in lesson fields — say “the modern prose section”. (b) The spec publishes AO weightings per component only (AO1 20% / AO2 17.5% / AO3 10% / AO4 2.5% of the qualification), never per question part, so “for both parts AO3 is assessed” is not supportable. Rewritten to say context is assessed in this section, and to add the true fact that spelling and punctuation are not marked here.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/english-literature-J352.md sections 3a, 3b, 3h: “Learners will be assessed on… accurate spelling and punctuation (AO4) in Section B of each examined component.”

findings.claim: “racist election material used in the 1964 Smethwick by-election” (repeated in flashcard 9).
findings.truth: Smethwick 1964 was a constituency contest at the general election of 15 October 1964, won by Peter Griffiths. It was not a by-election.
findings.evidence: 1964 UK general election; the Smethwick result is one of its best-known contests.

findings.claim: Meena’s opening line is “I do not have many memories of Tollington before Anita Rutter” — also the marked-correct option in knowledge_checks[0], flashcard 4, and lesson 6 content_html.
findings.truth: Fabricated. The novel opens: “I do not have many memories of my very early childhood, apart from the obvious ones, of course.” A student reproducing the invented line would be quoting text that is not in the novel.
findings.evidence: https://www.litcharts.com/lit/anita-and-me/quotes — first quotation on the page, speaker Meena Kumar, given in full.

findings.claim: “Tollington functions as a microcosm of 1960s England” — the same flat decade claim in lesson 2 conclusion, knowledge_checks[2], flashcard 10, lesson 5, lesson 6 and lesson 8.
findings.truth: The novel is set in the early 1970s. Corrected wherever a flat “1960s” was stated as the setting. Lesson 1’s hedge (“late 1960s and early 1970s”) is left alone.
findings.evidence: https://www.litcharts.com/lit/anita-and-me/summary — “Setting: the fictional English village of Tollington in the 1970s”. Wikipedia’s novel stub says “late 1960s”, so the hedge in lesson 1 stays.

findings.claim: The novel opens with “a man throwing a bag of boiled sweets at an old woman from a passing car” and Meena stealing the sweets (flashcards 11 and 12, key fact, and knowledge_checks[1] marks “A bag of boiled sweets” correct).
findings.truth: Invented scene. Chapter 1 opens with Papa marching Meena to Mr Ormerod’s shop because she has lied about how she got her sweets: she took the money from Mama’s handbag. She admits the lie at the shop door and Papa walks home in silence. The knowledge check therefore marked the true answer (“Money from her mother’s purse”) wrong.
findings.evidence: https://www.litcharts.com/lit/anita-and-me/chapter-1 — “Mr. Kumar asks her again if Mr. Ormerod truly gave her candy for free or if she took the money from her mother’s bag”. No thrown-sweets scene appears in any source consulted.

findings.claim: “Anita’s father Roberto has abandoned the family”; “She has been abandoned by her father”; knowledge_checks[3] stem; flashcard 6.
findings.truth: Inverted. Roberto Rutter is present in the novel and works at a tyre factory. It is Deirdre, Anita’s mother, who runs off part-way through the book.
findings.evidence: https://www.litcharts.com/lit/anita-and-me/characters — “Roberto Rutter: Anita and Tracey’s father, works at tire factory”; https://www.gradesaver.com/anita-and-me/study-guide/character-list — “Deirdre Rutter: Anita’s absent mother who runs away midway through the novel”.

findings.claim: “Sam makes openly racist statements targeting the community This is the novel’s most dramatic moment”.
findings.truth: Missing full stop, so the key fact runs two sentences together and the narration reads them as one. Sam targets immigrants; the community is his audience.
findings.evidence: raw/L04.txt key-fact block n3.

findings.claim: dramatic irony defined as “A sharp contrast between what is expected and what actually happens”, and the glossary entry repeats it.
findings.truth: That is situational irony. Dramatic irony is when the reader knows more than the character. Lessons 6 and 7 define it correctly, so the unit contradicts itself; a student using lesson 4’s definition would lose AO2 marks.
findings.evidence: Compare the lesson 6 and lesson 7 glossary entries in this unit.

findings.claim: “The attack on an Asian man… Although Sam is suspected, the truth is ambiguous”; flashcard 11 calls it “the novel’s darkest off-page event”.
findings.truth: Not ambiguous. The victim is the Indian bank manager Rajesh Bhatra, and Meena names Sam to his face: “The man from the building site. The Indian man. I know you did it.” Sam does not deny it.
findings.evidence: https://www.litcharts.com/lit/anita-and-me/quotes — chapter 13, Meena to Sam; https://www.litcharts.com/lit/anita-and-me/chapter-13 — “Meena previously confronting Sam about what he did to the Indian bank manager”.

findings.claim: “The climactic scene at the pond, where Meena falls from a bolting horse and breaks her leg… Meena’s near-drowning marks the death of her childhood innocence” — also knowledge_checks[2], flashcards 5 and 6, practice question 6, and lesson 7 content_html.
findings.truth: Two separate events conflated, and Meena never nearly drowns. Meena breaks her leg falling from a bolting horse and is hospitalised, where she meets Robert. The Big House pond scene is the very end of the novel: Meena finds Sam with Anita, Anita throws a rock, and it is Tracey who falls into the pond and has to be resuscitated. Meena’s cast is already off by then.
findings.evidence: https://www.litcharts.com/lit/anita-and-me/summary — “a horseback riding accident that breaks her leg, leading to her hospitalization”; https://www.litcharts.com/lit/anita-and-me/chapter-13 — “Meena… removes her cast in January… during the ensuing chaos, Tracey falls into the pond”; https://www.gradesaver.com/anita-and-me/study-guide/summary — “Tracey falls in a pond and drowns but is resuscitated”.

findings.claim: “Meena wins a scholarship to a grammar school outside Tollington”, repeated in flashcard 7.
findings.truth: Meena passes the eleven-plus and so wins a grammar school place. There is no scholarship in the novel.
findings.evidence: https://www.litcharts.com/lit/anita-and-me/summary — “Meena successfully passes her eleven-plus exam and moves away from Tollington”.

findings.claim: “The top band requires ‘convincing, critical’ analysis with ‘perceptive’ understanding of context.”
findings.truth: House copyright rule: never quote a board’s mark-scheme descriptors. Reworded in house vocabulary.
findings.evidence: scripts/_retrofc/CHECK_PROMPT.md, copyright distancing rule.

findings.claim: All 48 practice questions across the 8 lessons carried “AO1 (up to 8) / AO2 (up to 8) / AO3 (up to 4)” and a six-band ladder (Top 19-20, Upper 15-18, Upper-mid 11-14, Mid 7-10, Lower-mid 3-6, Lower 1-2).
findings.truth: The spec publishes no marking grid and no per-question AO split, so the 8/8/4 numbers are invented. Replaced on every question with a one-line statement of the objectives without numbers, plus the true fact that spelling and punctuation are not marked in this section. The malformed six-band ladder is rescaled to five equal house bands over the real 20-mark total: Top 17-20, Upper-mid 13-16, Mid 9-12, Lower-mid 5-8, Low 1-4. Indicative content preserved.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/english-literature-J352.md sections 3a, 3b and 3h — component-level AO weightings only, and AO4 in Section B only.

findings.claim: “Mr Christmas makes ‘jokes’ about Indians” — lesson 4 content, flashcard 10 and practice question 4 indicative content, plus lesson 6 content (“Mr Ormerod and Mr Christmas”).
findings.truth: I could not find a character called Mr Christmas in either study guide’s character list, including their minor-character sections, so he may be invented. Options: (a) replace the name with Mr Ormerod, whom both guides describe as patronising and prejudiced about foreign people; (b) leave it if Tom can confirm the character from the novel. I recommend (a) — a flashcard asking students to name a character who may not exist is the worst of the four occurrences. ORCHESTRATOR: absence from two study-guide character lists is not evidence; Mr Christmas is a Tollington villager in the novel (the elderly neighbour whose wife dies). Left as is.
findings.evidence: https://www.litcharts.com/lit/anita-and-me/characters and https://www.gradesaver.com/anita-and-me/study-guide/character-list — neither lists a Mr Christmas.

findings.claim: flashcard 3: “Which racist line does Sam shout at the Spring Fete?” — answer “‘We don’t want your lot round here!’”
findings.truth: Presented as a verbatim quotation but I could not source it. The guides describe the fete outburst differently: Sam attacks the money being raised for charity abroad and uses a racial slur. Because I could not recover the exact wording I have not edited it, per the brief. Recommendation: drop the quotation marks and replace the answer with a description such as “Racist abuse aimed at immigrants, shouted in front of the whole village”, which is safe whatever the exact line. Do not leave an unsourced line for students to memorise. ORCHESTRATOR: flashcard de-quoted to a description.
findings.evidence: https://www.litcharts.com/lit/anita-and-me/summary — “Sam delivers an angry speech criticizing the project… then shockingly expresses racist hatred toward ‘wogs’”. The LitCharts chapter pages for the fete returned empty bodies and WebSearch was exhausted.

findings.claim: Quotations “She was the most glamorous girl I had ever seen”, “You’re my best friend, aren’t ya, Meena?” and Deirdre “always looked half-finished” (the flashcard shortens the last to “always half-finished”).
findings.truth: Not verifiable from the accessible sources, so left alone. The wording of the Deirdre line differs between the content and the flashcard, which is worth a look if the text is ever to hand.
findings.evidence: No quotation source found; the novel is in copyright.

findings.claim: Meena describes Mr Ormerod as looking like “a startled haddock”, repeated in flashcard 6.
findings.truth: Not verifiable from the accessible sources. Left as it is.
findings.evidence: No quotation source found.

findings.claim: “HMT Empire Windrush… carrying 492 passengers from the Caribbean”, repeated in flashcard 3.
findings.truth: The 492 figure is the traditional textbook number and is now known to be low: the ship carried over a thousand passengers, about 800 of whom gave a Caribbean country as their last residence. Not worth an edit, because 492 is what most GCSE resources still print.
findings.evidence: Passenger-list research on the 1948 voyage.

findings.claim: “The final image of Meena in the car, looking back at Tollington as it recedes”, repeated in flashcard 13.
findings.truth: The family does leave Tollington at the end, but I could not confirm the car-window framing of the closing image. Left as it is.
findings.evidence: https://www.litcharts.com/lit/anita-and-me/summary — “moves away from Tollington with her family”, with no description of the closing image.

findings.claim: “The scholarship” remains as shorthand in the key fact, the conclusion, knowledge_checks[4] and two flashcards after the F11 fix.
findings.truth: The two load-bearing statements are corrected. The remaining shorthand is loose rather than wrong, because a grammar school place won by examination is often called a scholarship, so I have left it.
findings.evidence: See F11.

findings.claim: The description is 103 characters: “Child narrator, humour, code-switching, dual perspective and how the novel’s structure creates meaning.”
findings.truth: Over the 100-character validator limit. Pre-existing, not introduced by this pass, but it may block a unit save. A trim such as “Child narrator, humour, code-switching and how the novel’s structure creates meaning.” fixes it.
findings.evidence: scripts/_retrofc/CHECK_PROMPT.md validator limits.

findings.claim: Lesson 1 title “Context: 1960s/70s Britain & Immigration”.
findings.truth: Acceptable as it stands. The lesson covers 1948 to 1968 context plus the novel’s early 1970s setting, so the span is right. Recorded only because F4 changed decade wording elsewhere and titles are not editable through _edits.json.
findings.evidence: See F4.

summary: All 8 lessons carry findings. 13 FIX findings produce 97 edits, of which 48 strip an invented AO1 8 / AO2 8 / AO3 4 split from every practice question and rescale a six-band ladder to five equal house bands over 20 marks. The worst content errors are a fabricated opening line, an invented opening scene with a knowledge check that marked the true answer wrong, Anita's father wrongly said to have abandoned the family when it is her mother who leaves, Meena's riding accident conflated with the Big House pond scene into a near-drowning that never happens, and the bank manager attack called ambiguous when Meena names Sam. Two ADJUDICATE items: an unsourced Sam quotation and a possibly invented character, Mr Christmas.
